anomaly_def.Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Row-count and data-distribution metadata are stale or incomplete, causing systematic cardinality misestimation and poor plan choices.
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead logging path (log buffer, log files, archiver/replicator) is saturated or mis-configured, driving up commit latency and stalling write activity.

When these two root causes strike together, the database exhibits a mixture of optimizer-related and log-related symptoms that reinforce each other:  • Execution plans show grossly inaccurate estimates, leading to plan shapes that inflate redo generation (e.g., unnecessary row-by-row updates, wide nested loops, or missing batch merge operations).  • Concurrently, sessions accumulate high LOG* and COMMIT wait events, throughput collapses, and checkpoint or archival backlogs appear.  • Autovacuum/auto-stats or plan recompiles fire more often but finish later because they themselves suffer from log-flush delays.  • Spikes in buffer dirtiness, memory pressure from bloated hash/ sort operations, and lock contention extend transaction lifetimes, further multiplying log volume and commit queuing.  • Administrators may find it difficult to attribute slowdown to either the optimizer or the log subsystem alone because symptoms of one manifest as effects in the other.

Causal interaction: Stale or incomplete statistics mislead the optimizer into choosing row-oriented, non-batch, or overly parallel plans that touch many more rows than necessary, dramatically increasing redo generation and frequency of commits, thereby amplifying pressure on an already constrained log subsystem. The resulting log-write stalls prolong transaction duration and lock retention, preventing automatic statistics jobs from keeping pace with data changes and allowing statistics staleness to deepen. The feedback loop between inaccurate statistics (producing write-heavy, long-running plans) and log bottlenecks (delaying stats refreshes and transactional completion) spirals into severe throughput degradation and unpredictable query latency.

entry.official_definition: The length of time in seconds an InnoDB transaction waits for a row lock before giving up.
entry.trigger_condition: An InnoDB transaction waits longer than innodb_lock_wait_timeout for a row lock.
entry.workload_impact: The lock wait gives up; by default only the current statement is rolled back unless innodb_rollback_on_timeout is enabled.
entry.default_behavior: Defined as an InnoDB system variable.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when a statement cannot obtain the required lock within the configured waiting window because another transaction or metadata operation is holding an incompatible lock.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect blocking sessions, reduce conflicting transaction overlap, shorten transaction lifetime, and review lock scheduling and schema-change timing.
